brewing_context.title: Role of coffee in daily life

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's home brewing context — frequency, occasions, and household role — then moves through the acquisition journey, from trigger to channel to spend, before probing the specific product requirements and trade-offs that define their ideal machine. It closes with satisfaction, pain points, and future intent, allowing the data to separate the five segments on the basis of their brewing behaviour, purchase drivers, and priorities.
metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on brewing habits, machine type and usage, purchase drivers, and satisfaction with key machine attributes.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Usage/behavioural combined with jobs-to-be-done: the primary axis is how the machine is used (daily ritual vs. convenience vs. specialty pursuit) and what job it is hired to do (quick caffeine, milk-based drinks, espresso craft, family volume). segments.name: Daily Ritualists
segments.description: Brew multiple cups every day, treat the machine as a central kitchen appliance, and value speed and consistency over experimentation. They are the heaviest users and often own a drip or pod machine.
segments.hypothesis: They will report the highest daily frequency, prioritize fast heat-up and quiet operation, and be less willing to trade convenience for specialty features.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Users
segments.description: Brew one or two cups daily, primarily for a quick caffeine fix, and rely on pod or super-automatic machines. They value one-touch operation and minimal cleanup over brew quality.
segments.hypothesis: They will show high satisfaction with pod machines, low interest in manual brewing, and cite convenience as the top purchase driver.

segments.name: Specialty Users
segments.description: Actively pursue better coffee at home, own espresso or manual machines, and enjoy experimenting with beans and brew methods. They are willing to invest time and money for quality.
segments.hypothesis: They will report higher spend, more manual brew methods, and rate brew quality and versatility as more important than convenience.

segments.name: Family Volume Brewers
segments.description: Brew for multiple household members, often in large batches, and need a machine that can keep up with volume. They prioritize capacity, counter space, and durability.
segments.hypothesis: They will report brewing for 3+ people, prefer drip machines with large carafes, and cite counter space and build quality as key pain points.

segments.name: Occasional Users
segments.description: Brew only a few times a week, often on weekends or for guests, and have low engagement with the category. They may own a basic machine and are not invested in upgrading.
segments.hypothesis: They will report low frequency, low spend, and low interest in new features; they are the least likely to replace their machine soon.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question cp8 (role of coffee in daily routine) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it explicitly asks respondents to categorize their relationship with coffee, cleanly separating ritual, caffeine fix, hobby, family, and occasional treat.
notes: Family volume brewers are identified by household size and capacity-related preferences; they may also brew multiple cups but not necessarily for themselves.
Occasional users are identified by low frequency, guest-oriented brewing, and low spend.
Specialty enthusiasts are identified by manual/espresso machines, high spend, and desire for variety and quality.
Convenience-driven users are identified by pod/super-auto machines, quick caffeine fix, and acceptance of worse coffee for convenience.
Daily ritualists are identified by high daily volume, morning ritual, and sensitivity to speed.
6 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
